title: Step-by-Step Guide for Making a Custom Yoyo Pouch
content:
Someone recently asked me about this leather yoyo pouch that I made back in 2017. At the time, I had posted a step-by-step tutorial for making one on the r/Throwers reddit page. The Imgur link I used there is now down but I still had the draft write up of this post, so I figured I would share it here for posterity/archive purposes.

“I was looking around for a nice case to carry around my fav yoyos but everything I could find seemed to be square shaped, repurposed and didn’t fit the shape of a yoyo. I wanted something that was practical, looked nice and protected my yoyo from dinging against door frames :P. So I decided to come up with my own design. Here is a tutorial for anyone who would like to make one for themselves. 

Materials:

Fabric: Material of choice, I recommend leather or a vinyl pleather (easier for punching holes). Can be found at a craft store like Michaels or Tandy Leather. You will need at least 8” x 8”. The piece I bought was 8 1/2” x 11”.

550 paracord

Carabiner

Cordlock

Yoyo(s) of choice

Hole puncher, an awl or a nail (a hole puncher will make nicer looking holes though)

Heavy duty thread (I like Gütermann upholstery thread)

Heavy needle (or sewing machine)

Scissors

Marker

Lighter (optional)

Thimble (optional)/ I like to use a piece of plywood to help push the needle through the leather.

Lighter (optional) for melting thread and paracord ends

Spring clip (optional)

Base of pouch: Trace out the circumference of the yoyo, leave an extra 1/8th inch of space around the yoyo. A looser fit will be easier to pull the yoyo out and will allow the pouch to fit a wider range of yoyos. A tighter fit will have a cleaner/ tailored look.

Side of pouch: Cut a rectangular piece of leather that is about 8 1/2” long (depending on the circumference of the base, leaving a bit of error room). Cut the height of strip by adding 1 1/4” to the height of your yoyo (this worked out to be around 3 1/8” for mine).

Sewing: To make clean stitches, sew the pieces together inside-out, placing stitched about 1/16” from the edge, following around the edge of the circular base.

Note: I don’t currently have a sewing machine and sew everything by hand (which has a nice aesthetic but takes A LONG TIME). If you have a sewing machine, it will make one of these waaaaayyy faster!

I had about an extra 1/2” that I trimmed off.

Use a spring clip to keep the edges straight while stitching.

I recommend leaving 3/4 to 1” unstitched to provide space for pulling the yoyo out of the case. I also doubled back the stitching at the end to provide more strength.

Use the hole punch to cut 8 to 10 evenly spaced holes about 1/4” from the top of the pouch.

Make the paracord long enough for the top of the pouch to open up wider than the yoyo.

The pouch can either be worn to hang long or short by clipping through one of the loops of paracord.”

Feel free to reach out if you have any questions or suggestions!

title: The Eugene Disruption: Dissecting the Lineage, Retail Politics, and Ideological Feud Between YoYoFactory and One Drop YoYos
content:
Executive summary

The rivalry between YoYoFactory (YYF) and One Drop YoYos is among the most consequential cultural and industrial conflicts in modern yo-yo history. Originating during the transition to unresponsive, high-performance metal yo-yos (2007–2009), the clash was fueled by three interconnected flashpoints:


  Design lineage disputes: the controversy surrounding the unreleased Buzz-On DV8, One Drop's The Project, and YoYoFactory's DV888.
  Economic disruption & retail wars: One Drop's domestic $60 price point collapsing the high-end metal market margin, leading to distributor pressure.
  Contrasting manufacturing philosophies: globalized, contest-driven mass production versus localized, machinist-led craft.


Act I: The unreleased precursor (the Buzz-On DV8)

In the mid-2000s, competitive yo-yoing was moving beyond plastic hybrids. Buzz-On Industries—co-founded by Dave Bazan and Dave Muehlhaeusler (popularly known as Dave Lahr)—held a central place among enthusiast modders.


  
    Mid-2000s: Buzz-On DV8 prototype
    Pre-production run limited by patent disputes
  
  ▼
  
    
      2007: One Drop "The Project"
      
        Colin Leland & Shawn Nelson CAD
        Aerospace hex-nut axle capture
        $60–$75, domestic in-house CNC
      
    
    
      2008: YoYoFactory "DV888"
      
        Officially licensed from Buzz-On
        Blended with 888 profile
        Global mass-production run
      
    
  


Buzz-On developed a pre-production all-metal, compact prototype with broad, flat rims called the DV8. However, due to industry patent disputes regarding weight-ring distribution (most notably YoYoJam's patent on plastic bodies with denser outer rims) and manufacturing hurdles, the DV8 never reached full commercial release; only roughly 100 numbered pre-production units were made. Despite its limited run, the compact, rim-weighted silhouette became legendary among competitive throwers.

Act II: The student, the machinist, and The Project (2007)

One Drop Design began in 2001 in Eugene, Oregon, as a contracting machine shop founded by Shawn Nelson and David Metz. While they had considered machining yo-yos as early as 2002, the project only materialized in 2007 when Colin Leland, a University of Oregon student, walked into their shop with a yo-yo concept.


  
    
      
        The Project's design DNA
      
    
  
  
    
      
        Colin Leland(Designer)
      
      
        Shape concept, silicone pad recess, perimeter rubber nubs, named "Project" (to cast light)
      
    
    
      
        Shawn Nelson(Lead Machinist)
      
      
        Aerospace-derived hex-nut capture system ("Never thread directly into aluminum")
      
    
    
      
        Mark Montgomery(2003 AP Champion)
      
      
        Influenced design tastes via former Buzz-On sponsorship; led to 2008 MarkMont Project
      
    
  


Deconstructing the "copy" myth

Community rumors long maintained that One Drop simply duplicated the Buzz-On DV8 without permission. While the aesthetic similarities were undeniable, the engineering reality differed:


  Aerospace axle architecture: Shawn Nelson noted that because of his background in aerospace manufacturing—where threading steel hardware directly into soft aluminum is avoided—he insisted on an internal nut capture system. When proposed, Leland famously asked, "How do you drill a hexagonal hole?!"
  Original geometry: Leland designed the profile, the silicone response grooves, and the signature push-in rubber rim nubs.


Addressing the legacy in modern retrospectives, One Drop co-founder David Metz explicitly stated:


  "The Project was not a copy of the DV8."
  — David Metz (da5id), One Drop YoYos


The confusion was further amplified by Mark Montgomery (2003 AP World Champion). Formerly sponsored by Buzz-On, Montgomery was an outspoken advocate for the DV8's profile. When Montgomery joined One Drop, his preferences helped shape the MarkMont Project (2008)—a widened, nickel-plated iteration—cementing the public association between the two companies' designs.

Act III: The $60 disruption & retail cold war

When The Project dropped in late 2007, high-end aluminum metal yo-yos routinely retailed between $100 and $150. Brands relied on standard distribution models: boutique runs outsourced to third-party machine shops, marked up for wholesale, and marked up again for retail.

One Drop disrupted this pricing model:


  Vertical integration: because Nelson and Metz owned their CNC mill and lathe equipment, they eliminated third-party machining margins.
  The $60 price point: One Drop brought The Project to market at roughly $60–$75, proving that an American-made, high-tolerance metal throw could be sold at a fraction of the prevailing market rate.


This pricing strategy disrupted major distributors and established brands, particularly YoYoFactory, which was aggressively scaling its own global catalog.

According to long-standing industry accounts and retail retrospectives, YoYoFactory put significant pressure on specialized distributors (such as YoYoExpert). YYF allegedly threatened to pull its high-volume product line from retail shelves if stores carried One Drop, fearing that a $60 baseline for domestic metals would deflate wholesale margins and erode the premium image of existing competition lines.

Act IV: The counter-strike & the DV888 (2008)

Recognizing both the market appetite for compact, affordable metals and the lingering IP debates, YoYoFactory's leadership (Hans Van Dan Elzen and Ben McPhee) executed a swift counter-strategy:


  
    Buzz-On licensing agreement
    +
    YYF 888 profile DNA
  
  ▼
  
    YoYoFactory DV888 (2008)
  
  ▼
  
    
      Retail positioning
      Positioned as the "official" successor to the Buzz-On DV8.
    
    
      Production shift
      Mass-produced in China to dominate the sub-$50 market.
    
  



  Official licensing: YYF partnered directly with Dave Lahr/Buzz-On to formally license the DV8 name and design language, effectively branding their release as the sole "legitimate" successor to the lineage.
  Hybrid design: YYF merged the DV8 profile with elements from their flagship metal, the 888, producing the DV888.
  Mass production: unlike One Drop's domestic machine shop model, YYF manufactured the DV888 in large quantities in China, driving the price down even further and turning the model into one of the best-selling metal yo-yos in history.


Act V: Two irreconcilable philosophies

The DV8/Project feud crystallized two fundamentally different visions of the modern yo-yo business:


  
    
      Structural dimension
      One Drop YoYos
      YoYoFactory
    
  
  
    
      Machining model
      100% in-house CNC shop (Eugene, Oregon)
      Global outsourced manufacturing (Shenzhen, China)
    
    
      Axle engineering
      Hex-nut capture → Modular Side Effects system
      Standardized set screws & press-fit hubstacks
    
    
      Market strategy
      Small-batch enthusiast drops, community direct sales
      Mass-market toy retail, contest sponsorships, global team
    
    
      Brand ethos
      Machinist-led, roots-inspired boutique
      Competitive powerhouse, high-volume market saturation
    
  


Cultural detail: the "One Drop" moniker

One Drop's identity was rooted in independence. Founders Metz and Nelson, both former musicians in reggae bands, named the company after the "One Drop" rhythm—the signature roots reggae drum cadence popularized by Carlton Barrett of Bob Marley and the Wailers. As David Metz explained, the beat is "technically simple, but very difficult to play with the right feel"—a metaphor for their approach to CNC machining.

title: The Evolution of Spin: A Material History of the Yoyo
content:
For as long as humans have been tossing spinning objects at the end of a string, the soul of a yoyo has been defined by what it is made of. The material dictates not only the weight and balance but the very sound, feel, and capability of the return top. From the earthy thud of catching a wooden classic to the high-pitched hum of modern aerospace-grade alloys, the evolution of yoyo materials is the evolution of the trick itself.

Here is the story of how the yoyo transformed from a simple wooden toy into a precision-engineered instrument.

The Wooden Era: The Roots of Spin

Before the mid-20th century, if you were throwing a yoyo, you were throwing wood. Historically, ancient yoyos may have been crafted from terracotta or stone, but the modern yoyo craze was built on the backs of hardwoods.

Manufacturers like Duncan and Flores relied heavily on hard maple. Maple offered a brilliant balance of durability and weight, and because these early yoyos featured a wooden fixed axle (the string looped directly around the wooden peg in the center), the natural friction of the wood was essential. It allowed the yoyo to sleep, but also gave it the "grab" needed to return to the hand with a simple tug.

Even today, fixed-axle purists seek out specific woods—like ash, mahogany, or walnut—for their unique aesthetics and play characteristics, cherishing the nostalgic, organic feel that only wood can provide.

The Plastic Revolution: Shaping the Future

As the 1950s and 60s rolled around, injection-molded plastics changed the world, and the yoyo industry eagerly followed suit. Plastic offered three massive advantages: mass production, unparalleled durability, and the ability to mold complex shapes.

Polystyrene: Early plastic yoyos were often made of polystyrene. While slightly brittle, it allowed for the mass production of iconic models like the Duncan Imperial.

Polycarbonate (Lexan): As string tricks evolved, players needed yoyos that wouldn't shatter when hitting the ground. Polycarbonate, known for its incredible impact resistance, became the standard for heavy-duty play.

Acetal/Delrin (POM): Later in the timeline, manufacturers turned to machined plastics like Delrin. Known for its extremely low friction and silky-smooth texture, Delrin is still used today to create premium plastic yoyos that rival the performance of metals.

The shift to plastic also allowed for the creation of the wide "Butterfly" shape, a structural innovation that would have been incredibly difficult and prone to breaking if carved from wood. This shape paved the way for modern string tricks.

The Age of Aluminum: Precision and Performance

The late 1990s and early 2000s marked the greatest leap in yoyo evolution: the popularization of the precision-machined aluminum yoyo. Once ball-bearing axles were introduced, players realized that spin times were no longer limited by axle friction, but by weight distribution and balance.

Metals allowed designers to push weight to the absolute outer rims of the yoyo, vastly increasing the moment of inertia and resulting in spin times that measured in minutes, not seconds.

6061 Aluminum: The workhorse of the modern yoyo industry. It is affordable, highly machinable, and takes anodization beautifully, allowing for the stunning colorways and splashes seen in modern collections.

7075 Aluminum: A denser, stronger aerospace-grade alloy. Because it is more rigid, designers can machine the walls of the yoyo incredibly thin, pushing even more weight to the rims for ultimate stability.

The Bimetal Breakthrough: Maximizing Rim Weight

If aluminum pushed the boundaries of rim weight, bimetal designs shattered them. In the 2010s, competitive players began demanding even more stability to execute highly complex, horizontal, and rapid-fire tricks.

To achieve this, manufacturers combined a lightweight aluminum body with dense, heavy rings made of Stainless Steel or Brass, press-fitted onto the rims. By using two different materials, designers effectively "cheated" physics, creating an extreme weight distribution that an all-aluminum yoyo simply cannot replicate. Today, bimetals dominate the competitive stage.

The Pinnacle of Premium: Titanium and Beyond

For the ultimate yoyo connoisseur, there is titanium. Titanium is incredibly strong but less dense than steel. Its exceptionally high strength-to-weight ratio allows designers to machine the walls of the yoyo to paper-thin tolerances (sometimes less than half a millimeter thick) without sacrificing durability.

Titanium yoyos are notoriously difficult and expensive to manufacture, but they offer a unique, floaty feel on the string and produce a distinct, resonant "ping" when they hit the end of the string. As a bonus, when sparked against concrete, titanium yoyos throw brilliant white sparks—a favorite party trick among brave collectors.

The Unending Cycle

The history of yoyo materials is a feedback loop: new materials unlock new designs, new designs inspire new tricks, and new tricks demand even better materials. Whether you are throwing a fixed-axle wooden classic on a lazy Sunday or competing on the world stage with a precision-machined titanium-stainless-steel marvel, you are holding a piece of history. The spin remains the same, but the canvas has forever changed.

title: The Evolution of Spin: The Grip That Brings It Back
content:
For a yo-yo to actually be a yo-yo, it has to come back. While spinning at the end of a string is a beautiful display of physics, the magic happens in the return. For decades, the mechanism that commanded the yo-yo to climb back up the string—the "response system"—was practically an afterthought. Today, it is a micro-engineered component that defines how a yo-yo plays.

As the yo-yo evolved from a simple up-and-down toy to a freely spinning, ball-bearing-equipped instrument, the response system had to adapt. Here is the history of the friction that brings it all back home.

The Natural Era: Fixed Axles and Cotton

In the early days of wooden yo-yos, there was no separate response system. The axle itself, firmly fixed to the two halves of the yo-yo, did all the work.

When you threw a wooden yo-yo, the cotton string looped around the wooden axle would grip just enough to allow it to "sleep" (spin freely). When you gave the string a sharp tug, the momentary slack allowed the cotton fibers to catch on the spinning wood, winding the string and forcing the yo-yo back to your hand. It was an elegant, simple system, but it was limited by friction—too much grip and the yo-yo wouldn't sleep; too little, and it wouldn't return.

The Mechanical Leap: Starbursts

The revolution came in the 1990s with the widespread adoption of the transaxle and, eventually, the ball bearing. Suddenly, yo-yos could spin for minutes with practically zero friction. However, this created a new problem: the yo-yo was too smooth. Tugging the string did absolutely nothing.

To solve this, manufacturers molded Starbursts into the plastic halves of the yo-yo. These were raised, star-shaped ridges radiating outward from the center bearing.

How it worked: When the string was pulled, the slack would briefly touch these plastic teeth, catching the string and winding it up.

The drawback: Starbursts caused the string to wear out rapidly due to the aggressive plastic teeth constantly chewing on the fibers.

The Custom Grip: Brake Pads and Friction Stickers

As tricks became more advanced, players wanted smoother spins without the loud, grinding feel of starbursts. Enter the replaceable response system.

Pioneered by companies like Playmaxx (makers of the legendary ProYo and Bumblebee), Brake Pads were small die-cut rings of cork or rubberized cloth that stuck to the inner walls of the yo-yo around the axle.

The Advantage: They provided a buttery-smooth sleep, but grabbed the string fiercely when tugged.

The Legacy: This shifted the paradigm. Response systems became a "wear item" that players had to replace regularly, much like changing strings. It also allowed players to customize their yo-yo by using thicker or thinner stickers.

The Hybrid Era: Rubber O-Rings

In the early 2000s, yo-yo design was in a transitional phase. Players were experimenting with wider gaps and thicker strings. YoYoJam, a major innovator of the era, popularized the use of thick Rubber O-Rings seated inside a groove on the yo-yo wall.

O-rings offered an incredibly durable response that rarely needed replacing. They sat flush (or slightly protruding) from the yo-yo wall, providing a snappy return. However, as playstyles shifted toward highly complex string layering, thick rubber o-rings proved too "grabby," often causing the yo-yo to return unexpectedly and hit the player in the knuckles.

The Modern Standard: Silicone and Unresponsive Play

Today, the yo-yo world is dominated by "Unresponsive" play. Modern yo-yos will not return to the hand with a simple tug; they require a specialized string trick called a "bind" to force the string into the response system. For this to work perfectly, the response system must be completely flush with the yo-yo wall, providing zero friction during a sleep, but absolute grip during a bind.

Silicone proved to be the ultimate material.

Flowable Silicone: Early innovators literally used tubes of automotive windshield sealant, pouring liquid silicone into a recessed groove in the yo-yo and letting it cure overnight.

Pre-Molded Pads: Today, manufacturers produce standardized, die-cut silicone pads (often called CBC pads, Snow Tires, or Slim Pads). They are backed with adhesive, snap perfectly into the yo-yo's recess, and offer the absolute pinnacle of smooth, reliable, and bind-ready friction.

title: The Evolution of Spin: The Threads That Tie It All Together
content:
A yo-yo without a string is just a beautifully machined wheel. While collectors and players often obsess over the latest aerospace-grade alloys and bimetal weight distributions, the string is the unsung hero of the yo-yo world. It is the direct link between the player and the return top, the track upon which the yo-yo rides, and the medium through which every trick is executed.

Just as yo-yo bodies evolved from hard maple to titanium, the string has undergone its own quiet revolution. Here is the complete history of how the materials tying it all together have transformed over the decades.

The Early Luxuries and Workhorses: Silk and Cotton

In the very early days of yo-yoing, before mass production demanded cheap, durable materials, Silk was the ultimate premium string. Silk threads were incredibly smooth, offering an unmatched, frictionless feel on the finger and a beautiful natural sheen. However, silk was fundamentally impractical for the masses. It was far too expensive, and its delicate fibers wore down quickly under the friction of a spinning wooden axle.

Because of this, 100% Cotton became the undisputed king for the vast majority of yo-yo history. During the golden age of fixed-axle wooden yo-yos, cotton was an absolute necessity. It possesses the perfect natural texture to grip a wooden axle, providing the exact amount of friction required to make the yo-yo "sleep" and then quickly return to the hand with a sharp tug.

However, cotton has severe limitations. It absorbs sweat and oils from the hands, causing it to become grimy and lose its tension quickly. More importantly, the constant friction physically burns and wears through the cotton fibers.

The Golden Rule of Cotton: If you play with a 100% cotton string, you must change it frequently. Pushing a worn cotton string too far results in the dreaded "snap," sending a heavy yo-yo flying across the room.

The Semi-Synthetic Experiment: Rayon

As players looked for alternatives to cotton that might replicate the smooth, luxurious feel of silk without the astronomical cost, string makers experimented with Rayon.

Rayon is a semi-synthetic fiber made from regenerated cellulose (wood pulp). In the yo-yo world, rayon strings are famous for being incredibly soft on the hands and possessing a brilliant, jewel-like shine. Unfortunately, rayon's fatal flaw is its tensile strength. It is highly prone to breaking under sudden stress and stretches unpredictably, making it more of a boutique novelty for gentle play rather than a material suited for aggressive, modern trick routines.

The Bridge: 50/50 Cotton-Polyester Blends

As tricks became more complex in the late 1990s and players needed strings that would last longer than a few hours, manufacturers introduced the 50/50 blend.

By twisting cotton and polyester fibers together, string makers found a happy medium. The cotton provided the necessary grip for the response system to work, while the polyester vastly increased the string's tensile strength and longevity. For a long time, standard "Slick 6" or "Slick 8" strings (named for the number of threads used in the twist) were the absolute standard for ball-bearing yo-yos.

The Modern Standard: Polyester

When the yo-yo world made the leap to fully "unresponsive" play—where the yo-yo requires a special string trick called a "bind" to return to the hand—the need for the grip of cotton vanished. This ushered in the era of 100% polyester string, which remains the dominant material today. But not all polyester is created equal; the modern landscape is defined by how the fibers are formed.

Spun Polyester: This is made from short "staple" fibers that are spun together much like cotton. Because of these short fibers, spun poly feels fuzzy, soft, and remarkably similar to classic cotton. It provides excellent grip for tight binds and is gentle on the hands, though it tends to fray and lose its tension faster than continuous filaments.

Trilobal Polyester: This is the secret weapon of boutique string makers. Unlike standard round fibers, trilobal polyester is extruded as a continuous filament with a triangular microscopic cross-section. This shape gives the string a higher surface area and allows it to reflect light brilliantly, giving it a shiny, almost metallic look. Because it is a continuous filament, trilobal poly is incredibly strong, smooth, and handles friction exceptionally well. Most importantly, it holds an open loop in the air perfectly, making it the premier choice for complex "slack" and "whip" tricks.

Note: Never use 100% polyester string on a wooden fixed-axle yo-yo. The friction will melt the plastic fibers, causing the string to fuse and snap almost instantly.

The Premium Synthetics: Nylon and Beyond

As modern competitive yo-yoing pushes the boundaries of physics, tricks require the player to whip massive loops of string through the air. To do this effectively, the string needs a certain amount of stiffness and weight to travel through the air without collapsing.

Enter Nylon. Nylon strings (or nylon-polyester blends) represent the premium boutique tier of modern string making.

The "Whip" Factor: Nylon is heavier and slightly stiffer than polyester. When you whip a nylon string, it cuts through the air and holds its shape beautifully.

The "Bounce": Nylon has a slight elasticity to it, giving the yo-yo a soft, bouncy, and distinct feel when it lands on the string.

Longevity: Premium nylon strings can last incredibly long, often outliving standard polyester strings by a wide margin.

The Perfect Tension

Today, making yo-yo string has evolved from a simple industrial process into a highly respected artisan craft. Boutique string makers carefully blend spun poly, trilobal poly, and nylon threads, experimenting with thickness and twist rates to create the perfect feel. The string is no longer just a tether; it is a critical piece of performance equipment.

title: The Evolution of the Spin: A Guide to Competitive Yo-Yo Play Styles
content:
If you ask the average person on the street what a yo-yo is, they will likely picture a wooden toy simply going up and down. But for those in the community—and those browsing the records here at YoYoArchive—the modern yo-yo is an instrument of complex physics, high-speed choreography, and boundary-pushing innovation.

Competitive yo-yoing has evolved drastically since the boom of the late 1990s. Today, the World Yo-Yo Contest and regional competitions recognize five primary divisions of play, commonly referred to as 1A through 5A.

Here is a comprehensive breakdown of the different styles of play that define modern yo-yo competitions.

1A: Single Unresponsive (String Tricks)

The Standard of Modern Play

When you watch a modern yo-yo video online, you are almost certainly watching 1A. In this division, players use a single, "unresponsive" yo-yo. Unlike traditional yo-yos, an unresponsive yo-yo has a wide bearing and will not return to the hand with a simple tug. Instead, it spins indefinitely at the end of the string (a "sleeper") until the player performs a specific maneuver called a "bind" to force it back.

The Focus: Complex string mounts, slack tricks, lacerations, and rapid-fire technical combinations.

The Yo-Yo: Wide, butterfly-shaped, unresponsive, and typically made of precision-machined aluminum, bi-metal, or high-grade plastic.

Vibe: Highly technical, dense, and visually mesmerizing. 1A is the most popular and highly contested division in the world.

2A: Two Looping Yo-Yos (Double A)

The Speed of Sound

2A is often considered the most visually intense and difficult division to master. Players use two "responsive" yo-yos—one in each hand—that return immediately when tugged. The goal is to keep both yo-yos in constant, simultaneous motion, creating intricate looping patterns, wraps, and tangles without the strings catching.

The Focus: Symmetrical and asymmetrical looping, continuous motion, around-the-world variations, and fast-paced choreography.

The Yo-Yo: Narrow, modified-shape (often classic imperial or slightly rounded), highly responsive, and specifically tuned for consistent return times.

Vibe: Rhythmic, explosive, and relentlessly fast. It requires thousands of hours of muscle memory to prevent catastrophic tangles.

3A: Two Unresponsive Yo-Yos (Triple A)

The Ultimate Multitasking

Invented in the early 2000s, 3A takes the dual-wielding aspect of 2A and combines it with the unresponsive string tricks of 1A. Players control an unresponsive yo-yo in each hand, weaving the two strings together to create massive, intricate mounts and knot-like formations.

The Focus: Two-handed string tricks, kink mounts, spatial awareness, and preventing the two spinning metal objects from colliding.

The Yo-Yo: Two identical, unresponsive butterfly-shaped yo-yos (usually 1A yo-yos).

Vibe: Deliberate, highly complex, and punishing. A mistake in 3A doesn't just mean a missed trick; it often results in a massive knot or a loud, metal-on-metal collision.

4A: Offstring

Breaking the Tether

If you've ever seen a diabolo (Chinese yo-yo), 4A will look somewhat familiar. In the Offstring division, the yo-yo is not tied to the string at all. Players launch the yo-yo into the air, perform tricks while it is in free flight or bouncing across the string, and then catch it back on the string to bind and return it to the hand.

The Focus: Aerial acrobatics, whip catches, bounces, and large sweeping body movements.

The Yo-Yo: Oversized, highly durable, bouncy plastic (like Delrin or polycarbonate) designed to survive frequent drops to the stage floor.

Vibe: Theatrical, expansive, and high-risk. 4A players use the entire stage and rely on dramatic tosses that captivate audiences.

5A: Freehand (Counterweight)

The Unleashed String

Patented in 1999 by Steve Brown, 5A revolutionized the sport. In this style, the yo-yo string is not attached to the player's finger. Instead, it is attached to a small counterweight (usually a plastic die, ball, or small character figure). Players let go of the counterweight, allowing the yo-yo and the weight to swing around each other in complex, gravity-defying orbits.

The Focus: Aerial releases, 360-degree spatial play, nunchaku-like swinging patterns, and rapid transfers of momentum.

The Yo-Yo: A standard unresponsive 1A yo-yo paired with a counterweight.

Vibe: Flowing, dynamic, and rebellious. 5A completely changes the physics of yo-yoing, turning the string itself into a moving projectile.

The Specialty Divisions: Beyond the Big Five

While the 1A through 5A divisions test raw technical prowess within strict boundaries, the yo-yo community is diverse and expressive. To accommodate different demographics and creative philosophies, major competitions—including the World Yo-Yo Contest—feature special exhibition and non-championship divisions that have become massive crowd favorites.

Art & Performance (AP) Division

The Entertainer First

In the AP division, you are an entertainer first and a yo-yo player second. This is one of the longest-running "alternate" divisions, completely freeing competitors from the standard, strict technical point system. The yo-yo must still be an integral part of the performance, but players are encouraged to use it for comedy, drama, storytelling, or emotional expression.

The Focus: Choreography, creative use of the stage, synchronicity with music, and audience interaction.

The Format: Players or teams can compete using any style or combination of yo-yos, often incorporating elaborate costumes and props. Instead of a standard 1st, 2nd, or 3rd place, judges typically award specific honors like the Entertainment Award, Artistic Award, and Creativity Award.

Vibe: Theatrical, expressive, and highly unpredictable. AP routines range from hilarious comedy sketches to breathtaking, emotional dance performances.

Women's Division

Showcasing Top Talent

Historically, competitive yo-yoing has been overwhelmingly male-dominated. The Women's Division (or Women's Freestyle) was introduced to highlight, support, and encourage female participation at the highest levels of the sport. It has become a fiercely contested division featuring some of the most prominent and technically gifted players in the modern era.

The Focus: World-class technical execution, clean trick evaluation, and representation on the main stage.

The Format: Competitors perform a freestyle routine (usually two minutes) and can choose to play in any of the primary styles (1A through 5A). The scoring uses the same strict technical criteria as the main divisions.

Vibe: Empowering and heavily competitive. The players in this division frequently compete in the main 1A-5A divisions as well, using this freestyle to further cement their absolute mastery of the toy.

Over-40 Division

The Veterans of the Spin

Yo-yoing is a lifelong pursuit, but a 15-year-old and a 45-year-old often have very different play styles and physical stamina. The Over-40 division was created to spotlight the older generation of throwers, specifically honoring the veterans from the massive yo-yo boom of the late 1990s, as well as parents who picked up the hobby later in life.

The Focus: Legacy tricks, seasoned stage presence, and proving that precision and flow do not fade with age.

The Format: Competitors 40 years of age or older perform a mixed-style freestyle (choosing 1A-5A). Because different styles naturally generate different amounts of points (e.g., 2A generates points faster than 1A), a mathematical coefficient is applied to the final scores to normalize them and make the competition fair. It is often split into "Open Class" for casual/newer older players, and "Master Class" for former world champions and elite veterans.

Vibe: Nostalgic, respectful, and surprisingly intense. It is a celebration of the sport's history, giving the crowd a chance to cheer for the pioneers who helped build modern yo-yoing.

title: The Schmoove Groove
content:
Recently someone asked what the deal was about Schoove Grooves on the YoYoExpert Forums. There were plenty of great answers, but the best would be the genius behind the Groove, Doc Pop's, own explanation

.

As @fradiger mentioned, this page has some good info on Schmoove Grooves.

The basic idea was to remove string friction by reducing the amount of surface area the string could touch. On a high wall yo-yo with a narrow gap, a schmoove groove could really reduce the amount of surface that a string could rub on while sleeping.

I first talked about the idea on an old yo-yo forum (probably yoyoing.com’s old forum). Then a year later, I asked @Feralparrot to mod a Anti-Yo Fluchs and some YoYoJam yo-yos to add the grooves. I liked them and decided to make them a main feature of The End when we were working on those.

The word Schmoove (or Shmoove) was a stylish way to say “smooth”. It was a common meme-y way of speaking back in 2006-ish, similar to how some people say “smoov” these days. The goal was to make yo-yos play more smooth, so “Schmoove” made sense. I think the original name I used for these was “Shmoove Rings”, but that changed over time.

It would be hard to prove how much the reduced surface area affects play, but there was one research paper that a yo-yoer wrote about the effects Schmoove Grooves had in generating extra air friction, which could then help in keeping a loop open during a slackacide. It was a dissertation written by a grad student who was studying aerodynamics, but the paper is no longer available. Hopefully some other folks can help find some of the 3D models and other cool yo-yo images from that paper.

When we shipped The End with Schmoove Grooves, I thought they’d start appearing everywhere. They look awesome, they don’t add significant cost to production, and I believe they work really well. But it took years for other manufacturers to adopt the idea. Anti-Yo produced a yo-yo called the YWET that had an added groove, but they said it was for putting in a second o-ring to increase response.

Another attempt at keeping the string from rubbing against the inner was was to create a “bump” where the bearing and response sit, so it isn’t flush with the rest of the inner wall. CLWY may have been the first to add that bump to their design. This bump sort of looks like a step from the inner wall to the response area, and it creates a gap similar to what schmoove grooves try to do.

I believe A-RT was the first yo-yo company to finally add Schmoove Grooves to their designs, and that’s when it finally started catching on. This is also where the size of schmoove grooves started getting wider and wider. When I was exploring the idea, I was nervous about what the gap would do, so I ony removed little bits of inner wall, then left a bit sticking back up, before another section was removed. You could say it was a tepid way of reducing inner wall. But after A-RT started exploring the idea, the grooves started getting bigger and bigger, with no little walls sticking up between them. This is how we finally ended up on the great big schmoove grooves (or “schwalls” as some people call them).

I might be wrong on a few details here, so feel free to correct more or help fill in gaps.

title: Two Yo-Yos, One String: The Rise of Hydr0A
content:
Born from a late-2024 experiment by Australian maker Nic Conrick, Hydr0A transformed an obscure two-yo-yo concept into a teachable, evolving style built around fixed axles, responsive play, and controlled chaos.

At first glance, Hydr0A looks like a problem someone forgot to solve.

There are two yo-yos, one string, and no fixed point. Every throw sends one end of the system away while the other remains live in the player’s hand. Every catch changes which yo-yo is acting as the anchor. Loops reverse, mounts overlap, and the object that looked like a counterweight a moment ago suddenly becomes the active yo-yo.

Then the pattern reveals itself.

One yo-yo leaves as the other returns. Two arcs cross like circles in a diagram. A familiar trapeze becomes a moving target. Responsive regens, fixed-axle stalls, counterweight releases, and two-handed string geometry all begin to occupy the same space.

This is Hydr0A, the fixed-axle style founded by Adelaide-based artist, musician, and maker Nic Conrick. In less than two years, it has moved from a private joke to a named discipline with purpose-built sets, a growing trick vocabulary, a four-week community curriculum, and recognition from one of the world’s largest yo-yo retailers.

It is still small. It is also no longer hypothetical.

Before Hydr0A, There Was Hydra

The basic idea of attaching two yo-yos to opposite ends of a single string is much older than Hydr0A. The configuration was historically called Hydra, and forum records describe it as early as the late 1990s. One retrospective on the YoYoExpert forum says Hydra tricks appeared in the third issue of YoYo World Magazine in the winter of 1999. A surviving 2009 description is blunt: “Two yo-yos are attached at opposite ends of a single string.”

Hydra never disappeared completely, but it remained a fringe style. Players occasionally resurfaced the idea on forums, often comparing it to 3A or 5A and noting the difficulty of starting and controlling two yo-yos without a conventional string-hand anchor. Hubstacks and other assisted starts could make modern bearing yo-yos more practical, but the style never developed the broad instructional ladder that helped 1A through 5A grow.

As late as April 2024, a YoYoExpert discussion about playing “3A yoyo but 5A style” treated Hydra as an obscure answer to a theoretical question. One participant called it “somewhere inbetween 3A and 5A while also just totally being its own thing.” Another said the linked clip was the only example a quick search had produced.

That was the opening Conrick stepped into. He did not claim to have invented the two-yo-yos-on-one-string configuration. His innovation was to rebuild it around the assumptions and vocabulary of 0A: fixed axles, responsive returns, stalls, regens, and the tactile rhythm of old-school play.

The zero in Hydr0A makes that lineage visible.

The Joke That Worked

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jFhaExkvPMU

Conrick had already spent decades around yo-yos before Hydr0A emerged. A member of Team Throw-Yo and the maker behind CowClops, he was known for handmade wooden yo-yos, sculpted counterweights, experimental string, and a willingness to treat skill toys as a material rather than a finished category.

Hydr0A grew out of that same instinct.

In a March 2025 forum discussion, Conrick traced the beginning to his offhand practice in late 2024. “The Hydr0A started as a joke that wasn’t very funny and then actually worked,” he wrote. Elsewhere, he described it as an extension of counterweight 0A whose double mounts were beginning to move into 3A territory.

The first public traces appeared near the end of 2024. On December 29, Conrick posted that he was “really digging hydr0A” with a pair of square yo-yos. Roughly two weeks later, on January 15, 2025, he published a 97-second setup video titled This is Hydr0A style yoyo. Its description reduced the proposition to one line:

Two fixed axle yoyos with just one string.

That simplicity was important. Classic Hydra could look like a specialist’s stunt. Hydr0A could be assembled from two responsive yo-yos and a string. They did not even have to match. When a Fixed Axle February participant demonstrated the style with an unmatched pair, Conrick called it proof that identical yo-yos were unnecessary.

His early setup advice also gave the experiment repeatable parameters. For the first Hydr0A challenges, he recommended approximately 5A-length string: shorter than a typical 1A setup but longer than 2A string. He also identified one of the style’s core mechanical problems. Without intervention, consecutive loops naturally alternate direction. To keep them traveling the same way, the player manually flips the caught yo-yo 180 degrees, mimicking the rotation it would receive during a regen.

This was no longer merely two yo-yos tied together. It was the beginning of a technique.

What Makes Hydr0A Different

Hydr0A borrows from several established styles without behaving exactly like any of them.

From 0A, it takes fixed-axle response, stalls, regens, and the demand for deliberate string tension. From 5A, it takes the idea that the end of the string can move freely and become part of the trick. From 3A, it inherits intersecting planes, simultaneous mounts, and the problem of controlling two spinning bodies at once. Looping and juggling also enter the vocabulary as the player begins alternating throws and catches.

The key difference is that neither yo-yo is permanently assigned the role of throw, counterweight, or anchor. Those jobs can change several times within one sequence.

That makes even elementary tricks feel newly unstable. A trapeze requires the player to manage not only the landing yo-yo but also the yo-yo forming the far end of the string. A loop is also a handoff. A regen may redirect the entire system. A double mount can resemble 3A geometry, but both yo-yos remain connected by one continuous line.

Hydr0A is difficult, but its difficulty is legible. The player can isolate a breakaway, a catch, a stall, or a flip and practice it as a discrete action. That would become crucial when the style moved from Conrick’s hands into the community.

Fixed Axle February Changes Everything

The decisive moment arrived in February 2025, only weeks after Conrick’s setup video.

The YoYo Boomers Club included Hydr0A with CowClops as a dedicated series in its month-long Fixed Axle February event on the YoYoExpert forum. Hydr0A appeared beside established teachers and players including Ed Haponik, Jerrod, Dazzling Dave, and the event’s broader fixed-axle trick ladder. CowClops supplied a purpose-built Hydr0A pair as the series prize.

More importantly, Conrick supplied structure.

The series began with setup, Venn Diagram, and Staccato Loops. Week two added trapeze stalls and instant brother stalls. Week three introduced the Hydr0A Zipper. The final week expanded into mounts, including Twin Doughnuts, Twin Undermount, and an invitation for players to invent their own variation.

The names made the style memorable. The weekly schedule made it approachable. The prize gave participants a reason to try it, but the tutorials gave them a way to continue.

Forum posts show players working through the mechanics in real time. Henry, Michal Jánský, Collin, Vitalii, and others compared setups, posted attempts, and asked for clarification. Conrick answered with practical advice while keeping the rules loose. When Vitalii worried about variations or mistakes, Conrick replied that the style was only about six weeks old and that new variations were welcome.

By the end of the event, four users had submitted Hydr0A videos totaling 22 entries. That was a small fraction of the overall Fixed Axle February participation, but it represented something the earlier Hydra discussions lacked: multiple people learning a shared sequence from a named curriculum. Vitalii, posting as Spinstar, completed the series and won the CowClops Hydr0A set. A later Instagram unboxing thanked Conrick, the YoYo Boomers Club, and YoYoExpert, documenting the physical set leaving its maker and entering another player’s collection.

Hydr0A had crossed the line from demonstration to transmission.

A Style Needs More Than Tricks

New yo-yo styles rarely grow through technique alone. They need language, equipment, documentation, and a reason for players to identify with them.

Hydr0A accumulated all four quickly.

Conrick gave the style a recognizable trick vocabulary. CowClops produced matched wooden pairs and donated a set as a prize. Team Throw-Yo incorporated Hydr0A and CowClops artwork into merchandise in March 2025, giving the project a visual identity outside the tutorial videos. Forum participants created variations and demonstrated that the style worked with Duncan Butterflies, Imperials, ProYos, square yo-yos, and unmatched pairs.

The tutorials also continued after the event. In January 2026, Conrick published expanded lessons for One Hand Juggle and Venn Diagrams. The one-hand variation replaced the usual regen element with a hand switch, followed by a 180-degree flip and a deliberately soft throw. The updated Venn Diagram lesson described alternating breakaways in which one yo-yo is released before the other is caught.

On Instagram, Conrick pushed the style into non-dominant-hand juggling and continued testing it with different pairs. An August 2026 post described Hydr0A juggling with his non-dominant hand and tagged Joseph Stromme’s non-dominant-hand challenge. Another showed Hydr0A played with a pair of Spin Drifters.

The style was no longer confined to the trick list that introduced it.

From Adelaide to REWIND

The clearest sign of Hydr0A’s widening reach arrived on September 1, 2026.

Yo-Yo Store REWIND published tutorial number 990 in its long-running daily trick series: Hydr0A Loop & Warp Drive. The Instagram post and its YouTube counterpart used a pair of YoYoFactory Loop 720s and explicitly credited “Nicholas Conrick” as the trick’s inspiration.

The response also showed that the style had reached well beyond the original Fixed Axle February group. Within hours, the Instagram post had drawn hundreds of likes and multilingual comments. Doc Pop wrote that he had tried learning the style when Conrick first posted the tutorials, “but it’s so hard!” Other commenters immediately asked to see the idea expanded into double-hand play.

That credit matters. REWIND operates in Japan and the United States and has documented thousands of tricks for an international audience. Its channel had previously covered classic Hydra ideas as nostalgic, old-school techniques. Calling this tutorial Hydr0A, using responsive loopers, and crediting Conrick recognized the newer branch as something distinct.

The progression is striking. At the end of 2024, Conrick was experimenting with a pair of square yo-yos. Six weeks later, players on another continent were learning his trick series online. Less than two years after the first posts, an international retailer was teaching a Hydr0A trick under its own tutorial banner.

That is what the rise of a niche style looks like now. It does not require a sanctioned contest division or a mass-produced signature yo-yo. It requires a reproducible setup, a body of tricks, teachers, students, and enough documentation that the next player does not have to begin from zero.

Controlled Chaos

Hydr0A remains young, and its future is unwritten. It may stay rooted in fixed-axle gatherings and online trick circles. It may develop a deeper juggling vocabulary, split into responsive and unresponsive branches, or inspire purpose-built hardware. Its trick language will almost certainly change as more players discover motions its founder has not tried.

That openness is part of its appeal.

Conrick did not simply revive Hydra by replacing bearings with wooden axles. He found a different logic inside the same basic configuration. Responsive play made the catches meaningful. Fixed axles made stalls and regens central. Counterweight 0A supplied the conceptual starting point, while 3A, 5A, and looping offered directions for expansion.

The result feels both old and new: two yo-yos, one string, and a growing number of possibilities between them.

Hydr0A began as a joke that worked. Now it is a style other people can learn.

Hydr0A Timeline

Winter 1999: Tricks using the older Hydra configuration are reported in YoYo World Magazine issue 3.

March 2009: A YoYoExpert forum glossary describes Hydra as two yo-yos attached to opposite ends of one string.

April 2024: Forum users still discuss Hydra as an obscure hybrid between 3A and 5A.

Late 2024: Nic Conrick begins experimenting with a fixed-axle, 0A-derived version.

December 29, 2024: Conrick publicly mentions playing “hydr0A” with a pair of square yo-yos.

January 15, 2025: Conrick publishes his first concise Hydr0A setup video.

February 2025: Hydr0A receives a four-week tutorial series and dedicated prize drawing during Fixed Axle February.

March 2025: Spinstar is named winner of the Hydr0A series and receives a CowClops Hydr0A set; Team Throw-Yo releases Hydr0A-themed merchandise.

January 2026: Conrick publishes expanded tutorials for One Hand Juggle and Venn Diagrams.

August 2026: Conrick documents non-dominant-hand Hydr0A juggling and continued experimentation on Instagram.

September 1, 2026: Yo-Yo Store REWIND publishes Hydr0A Loop & Warp Drive on Instagram and YouTube, crediting Nicholas Conrick.

title: We Are Throwers: The Documentary Yo-Yoing Made About Itself
content:
Almost eighty years after its first American boom, the yo-yo has been many things: a nostalgia toy, a novelty premium, a contest event, a collector's obsession. We Are Throwers set out to document what it had become for the people still spinning one — not as an outside curiosity, but as a sport, an art form, and for some, simply a way of living.

Released in 2017, the 58-minute documentary was shot entirely by and for yo-yo players, filmed across the United States, Japan, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Iceland. It followed no single competitor's arc and crowned no champion. Instead it asked players from around the world why they still pick a string up off the floor.

A Love Letter, Crowdfunded

The film began as an Indiegogo campaign in May 2015, led by Polish filmmaker Piotrek Śmietana. The pitch was explicit about what it was not: not another highlight reel of contest freestyles, and not a film made by outsiders explaining the hobby to itself. YoYoNews described it at the time as "a love letter to the yoyo community," built from the perspective of the players making it.

Backer rewards leaned into that community-made identity rather than typical crowdfunding swag. Contributors could pledge for limited-edition YoYoRecreation Draupnirs, one-off anodizing test runs from CLYW, and gear from other manufacturers, alongside T-shirts and DVD copies of the finished film. Higher tiers promised a "THROWER edition" DVD bundled with a photobook and bonus footage from each country visited, and top backers were offered a highly limited collector's DVD or Blu-ray digipack with production stills and creator signatures.

Three Continents, No Single Star

Production stretched across multiple years and three continents. Reviewers and forum members who tracked the project noted its patient, wide-lens approach: no single player carries the story, and a large number of notable throwers appear across its runtime rather than one headline subject. Players credited in the finished film include John Ando, Eric Bergmann, Patrick Borgerding, and Sebastian Brock, among many others captured across the trip.

That structure was deliberate. Rather than build toward a single competitive climax, We Are Throwers used its travel across the U.S., Japan, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Iceland to show how differently the same string, weighted disc, and open floor could be used depending on who was holding it.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XrOGYuS0L-w

Launch and Reception

The finished film launched digitally on January 8, 2017, distributed through Reel House. Wide purchase and rental access followed on July 30, 2017 — $15 to buy, $6 to rent, delivered as a DRM-free 1080p MP4 compatible with Mac, iPad, and iPhone. YoYoExpert marked the release with limited-edition We Are Throwers merchandise, including branded shirts and a tie-in yo-yo edition.

Community reaction on the YoYoExpert forums was enthusiastic and fast. One early viewer called it "10/10 recommend — it far exceeded my expectations." Another wrote simply, "Bought. Watched. Loved." A third said they had already watched it twice, "interrupted by inspired throwing sessions" in between.

What it means to do this simple, complex, frustrating, zen-like and exciting thing.

That line, from a forum commenter describing the film's throughline, captured why the project resonated: it treated throwing itself, not competitive ranking, as the subject worth documenting.

From Paywall to Free

The film played the festival circuit in the years after release, including a nomination for Best Feature Film at The Monthly Film Festival's July–August 2017 edition, and picked up an IMDb user rating in the high 7s out of 10. By 2021, the paywall came down entirely — We Are Throwers became available for free streaming on its official site, closing the loop on a project that began as a community-funded love letter and ended as a freely shared piece of yo-yo history.

We Are Throwers Timeline

March 2015: A first trailer circulates ahead of the crowdfunding launch.

May 2015: Director Piotrek Śmietana launches the We Are Throwers Indiegogo campaign.

2015–2016: Production travels across the U.S., Japan, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Iceland.

January 8, 2017: The film launches digitally through Reel House.

July 30, 2017: Wide purchase/rental access opens at $15/$6; YoYoExpert releases tie-in merchandise.

July–August 2017: The film is a Best Feature Film nominee at The Monthly Film Festival.

2021: We Are Throwers becomes available to stream for free on its official site.
